name: Champagne Fairs, Medieval International Commerce
summary: The Champagne Fairs, six annual trade fairs at Troyes, Provins, Bar-sur-Aube, and Lagny, become the commercial center of western Europe. Italian merchants (Genoese, Venetian, Florentine) meet Flemish cloth merchants and German buyers in a regulated fair cycle that runs nearly year-round. The counts of Champagne guarantee merchants' safety and enforce contracts; the fair courts develop commercial law; letters of credit (lettres de foire) enable large transactions without moving physical currency.

_quarry.structural_significance: The Champagne Fairs create the first integrated European commercial market; Italian banking techniques (double-entry bookkeeping, bills of exchange, commercial credit) spread northward through the fairs; their decline (after 1300, as Genoese galley routes to Bruges replace overland routes) illustrates how commercial geography changes with transport technology; the fairs' legal innovations form the basis of European commercial law
